The population loss is already pointed at the right predictor. The remaining gap is misspecification inside the GRU, a few invalid experiments, and one high-|y| slice that still has real headroom.

## Part A — Ideas

**1. High-|y| specialist with a causal gate.** About 45% of metric weight sits in a slice whose WP is ~0.43 against ~0.74–0.81 elsewhere. Add a second head that trains only on rows with causal gate g(x)=P(|y|>c | x) above a fixed threshold, loss = WMSE, blend `p = (1-g)*p_base + g*p_jump` with g frozen from a small classifier. This allocates trunk capacity the shared WMSE fit never gives the tail. Test: reuse one baseline, fit the gate once, then two specialist blends (c at the 80th and 90th |y| percentile). Falsifier: specialist slice WP ≤ baseline slice WP on a second fold. Risk: g is weak, so the specialist trains on the wrong rows; a gate fit on true |y| is leakage.

**2. Fix the NLL experiment before abandoning it.** Gaussian NLL targets E[y|x], not E[|y|y|x]/E[|y||x]. The reported run also never tested that objective: global grad clip kept a mean-step factor of 0.04 against 0.99 for WMSE, so the mean head was frozen. Use |y|-weighted Gaussian NLL (same minimizer as WMSE) with variance detached, β∈{0, 0.5}, and a separate mean-gradient clip matched to WMSE. The variance head is then only a learned per-row step size. Test: 3 fits from one init — WMSE, β=0, β=0.5 — and log mean-grad norms. Falsifier: mean-grad norm stays <30% of the WMSE run, or both β runs lose ≥0.001 WP. Risk: ν-free Gaussian tails still mismodel jumps; cap log-variance to ±2.

**3. Sequence-capped EMA weight mass.** Per-batch weight mass already swings 0.1×–9.7×, so Adam’s effective LR tracks whichever sequences happen to hold the large |y| rows. Divide by an EMA of batch weight (population minimizer unchanged) and cap each sequence’s weight at the training p95. Test: 3 fits — per-batch sum, EMA only, EMA+cap — same data order. Falsifier: batch grad-norm CV drops <20% and fold WP moves <0.0005. Risk: the cap changes the population target; if a few sequences legitimately dominate the pooled correlation, the cap lowers the metric it is trying to raise.

**4. Equalize the two targets.** The metric averages two correlations. The trainer divides by w_t0+w_t1, so the heavier target owns the shared GRU. Normalize each target by its own weight sum, then average the two losses with fixed 1/2. Test: one diagnostic pass that only records loss-mass share, then 2 fits (pooled vs equal) if that share is outside 45–55%. Falsifier: mass share is already ~50/50, or per-target WP moves <0.001. Risk: the heavier target was heavier because it is the identifiable one; equalizing spends capacity on noise.

**5. Shared latent price, separate WP links.** Structurally t0+t1 = bid−ask, a current quantity, while (t0−t1)/2 carries F. The WP-optimal maps are not that identity, because |t0| and |t1| reweight different rows — which is why a sum-to-zero head lost 0.0016. Predict one latent z, set `p_k = a_k + b_k z` with (a_k, b_k) global per target (the metric’s legal invariance), and train WMSE on both targets through that map. Test: 2 fits, tied latent vs two free heads, same parameter budget. Falsifier: tied model loses ≥0.001 on the sum of the two target WPs, or the free model’s p0+p1 already matches −spread to within 0.01 on scored rows. Risk: anonymous features do not identify the spread, so the hard tie is wrong and only the soft version is informative.

**6. Sign loss on the tail.** With w=|y|, a sign error at |y|≈2 costs as much as many small rows. Split `p = m * tanh(s)`, train weighted BCE on sign(y) with weight |y| only for |y|>0.5, and WMSE on m. Global affine still absorbs scale. Test: 2 fits against WMSE; report sign accuracy for |y|>1 and slice WP. Falsifier: sign accuracy on |y|>1 rises <2 points and slice WP rises <0.01. Risk: sign(y) near the threshold is noise; the mask has to stay off the label-floor rows that currently carry teacher signal.

**7. Pooled correlation on accumulated statistics, not per chunk.** Per-chunk WP lost because a chunk has too few scored rows and a noisy correlation gradient. Keep WMSE as the stable term and add λ=0.1 times a correlation gradient from sufficient statistics accumulated over 32 sequences (Σw, Σwy, Σwp, Σwyp, Σwp², Σwy²), then reset. Same population target as the metric, lower gradient variance than chunk Pearson. Test: 2 fits, λ=0.1 and 0.3, against WMSE. Falsifier: training WP and validation WP rank the three runs identically within 0.0005. Risk: accumulated stats go stale across regime shifts; a bad λ recreates the September result.

**8. Group DRO across volatility bins, aimed at transfer.** Local F0 sits near 0.682 and public near 0.668. That 0.013 gap is about ten times seed noise and three times the entire rank-22-to-rank-1 spread. ERM fits the bins that dominate |y| mass. Minimize the worst of four causal volatility bins plus the mean. Test: 3 fits — ERM, DRO with group weight 0.25, DRO at 0.5 — and publish worst-bin WP beside mean WP. Falsifier: worst-bin WP is flat and mean WP drops >0.002. Risk: DRO underfits the high-|y| bin, which is exactly the bin that pays.

**9. Unconventional — distill the early teacher’s hidden state, and stop blending its labels.** A teacher with validation WP 0.2–0.4 blended at a=0.9 is a memorizer label. Keep a=0 on labels. Add λ‖h_student − P h_teacher‖² from the best validation-WP epoch of a small transformer, P a fixed projection. The student loss stays WMSE on y. Test: 3 student fits — no teacher, a=0.9 label blend from that early epoch, feature distill only. One teacher, stopped at peak validation WP, every epoch kept. Falsifier: feature distill does not beat “no teacher” by 0.001 on a second fold. Risk: a 0.4-WP teacher has nothing in its state worth copying; λ then only regularizes toward junk.

## Part B — Red team

**Why those losses failed.** The consistency claim is right at the population, unrestricted, pre-clip level, and wrong as an account of these runs.

NLL was not a negative result. The clip factor says the mean parameters received about 4% of a real step, and the unweighted Gaussian mean is a different functional from the |y|-reweighted mean whenever residual scale depends on x. β-NLL repairs the clip, not the target. Until idea 2 is run, “NLL does not help” is an optimization incident.

Per-chunk Pearson failed as an estimator. Chunk-level correlation with sparse `is_scored` rows has a huge variance and a flat gradient whenever the chunk prediction is nearly constant. That does not mean a pooled correlation built from enough scored rows is useless. It does mean another mixing ratio on the same chunk loss will lose again.

Distillation-loss variants were second-order. At a=0.9 the label is already the teacher, so swapping MSE for a Pearson or difference-channel match cannot move the student much. The variants that did move teachers — propensity 0, a floor on zero labels, class-3 upweight — change which rows count, i.e. the measure, not the distance. Sum-to-zero lost 0.0016 because it contradicts t0+t1=−spread and also contradicts the two different |y| reweightings. Muon’s −0.005 with a higher stable rank says this GRU is optimization-stable and prior-limited; a better-conditioned optimizer is not the bottleneck.

The variance-limited story does not survive the slice numbers. Seed noise of 0.0007–0.0014 is the noise of the pooled endpoint. It is not a floor under a slice that scores 0.43 with an oracle readout of 0.968. Those cannot both be “the metric is maxed, only noise remains.”

**What the B300 runs say.** Train WMSE 0.01 against validation WMSE ~1.55, with validation WP falling every saved epoch, is memorization. A zero prediction has weighted MSE of order 1 on labels inside [−2, 2], so 1.55 is worse than predicting nothing, while 0.01 is fit to noise. Tokens are not the binding count: 10,607 sequences and a sparse scored mask are a small label set next to 0.63–1.54B parameters at LR 3e-4 for 30 epochs. The 1.54B net scoring 0.31–0.41 against the 630M net’s 0.16–0.17 only says the larger net had not finished forgetting yet. Overwriting early epochs destroyed the only checkpoints that could have been teachers. A GRU at ~0.68 is the stronger teacher today.

Redesign: models small enough to beat the GRU on validation WP before any width doubling; LR nearer 1e-4 with warmup and decay; select and keep every epoch on validation WP, not train WMSE; dropout or drop-path on by default; |y|×propensity weights identical to the student; no label blend unless teacher validation WP exceeds the student. Feature distillation (idea 9) is the only use of a weaker teacher.

**Most likely wrong assumption.** That the 0.968 oracle branch readout is a causal upper bound. If the branch index is a function of |y|, the readout is fit on a y-selected subset and estimates a different conditional. It does not imply a causal gate can reach anything near 0.968, and it makes the “representation is solved, route the loss” moral much stronger than the evidence. Second, and operationally costly: treating a single exposed F0 endpoint as the decision metric. The local–public gap is ~0.013. A loss change of +0.001 on F0 is below the transfer gap and inside seed noise, so most of the loss program is aimed at a quantity that does not decide the leaderboard.

**Stop.** Stop 30-epoch 3e-4 transformer runs and stop overwriting checkpoints. Stop a=0.9 label blends from any teacher whose validation WP is below the student’s. Stop reading the clipped NLL run as evidence about heteroscedastic objectives. Stop sum-to-zero target constraints. Stop Muon on this GRU. Stop full-endpoint contests for expected gains under ~0.001 that lack a pre-registered high-|y| slice metric, a second fold, and two seeds. Stop adding new distance functions on top of a=0.9 distillation; change the row measure or the parameter sharing, and test that change with a=0.
